intro: Most people never see a big game in person. They hear it, watch it or catch a short clip of it. In 1921 a Pittsburgh radio station carried a baseball game for the first time. By 1960 almost nine in ten American homes had a television. By 1979 a cable channel showed highlights all day and night. Each new way of sending a game changed who could follow it and what they remembered.

Records work the same way. A record looks like a plain number, such as 60 home runs or 8.90 meters. Behind every number sit choices: how the time was measured, how strong the wind was, what equipment was allowed, which drugs were tested for and which athletes were allowed to compete at all.

In this unit you will trace sport from the telegraph wire to the replay booth. You will read laws, rule books and rulings about records. You will be able to explain how media shaped memory and why a record can be an argument, and you will support your answer with dates and documents.
bigQuestion: How do the ways we send and count a game shape what we remember and what we believe is the best ever?

timeline.t: The IAAF is founded and begins ratifying world records
KDKA in Pittsburgh carries a major league game on radio
NBC carries the Rose Bowl coast to coast
First televised baseball games in New York
Frick lists Maris's 61 home runs separately; Sports Broadcasting Act signed
CBS shows the first instant replay in a live telecast
IOC tests athletes at the Games; Beamon jumps 8.90 m in Mexico City
ESPN goes on the air from Bristol, Connecticut
Redesigned men's javelin; NFL first uses replay review
Ben Johnson stripped of Olympic gold in Seoul
MLB recognizes seven Negro Leagues as major leagues

words.d: a radio broadcast in which an announcer described a distant game from telegraph reports
a group of stations linked to carry the same program at the same time
money a broadcaster pays for permission to show or carry games
laws that stop businesses from joining together to limit competition
a rule keeping a game off local television, often to protect ticket sales
a recording of a play shown again seconds after it happens

to check and officially approve, as a governing body does with a record

test.q: What did radio announcers use to re-create distant games?
test.why: Re-creations were built from short telegraph messages sent from the ballpark.

test.q: Which Chicago owner let many stations carry his team's games in the 1920s?
test.why: Cubs owner William Wrigley Jr. opened the airwaves and charged no fee.

test.q: Why was the 1927 Rose Bowl broadcast important?
choices: It was the first coast-to-coast sports broadcast on a network
It was the first televised game
test.why: NBC carried it across the country, linking many stations at once.

test.q: What problem did the Sports Broadcasting Act of 1961 solve for leagues?
choices: It let leagues pool television rights without breaking antitrust law
test.why: A judge had blocked the NFL's pooled deal; the act made such deals legal.

test.q: Why did CBS and NBC both show Super Bowl I?
choices: Each held rights to one of the two leagues
It was shown only on radio
test.why: CBS had NFL rights and NBC had AFL rights.

choices: The first instant replay was shown in a live telecast
test.why: Tony Verna replayed an Army touchdown during the Army–Navy game on CBS.

test.q: Which statement best describes how the 1951 Giants–Dodgers game is remembered?
choices: Through a short recording of the radio call
test.why: A listener's recording of Russ Hodges's call became the main memory of the game.

test.q: From 1977, what timing did the IAAF require for sprint world records?
test.why: Sprint records needed fully automatic timing from 1977.

test.q: What makes a sprint mark wind-aided?
choices: A tailwind above 2.0 meters per second
test.why: A tailwind over 2.0 meters per second keeps a mark off the record list.

test.q: Why did Bob Beamon's 1968 jump spark debate?
choices: He jumped in thin air at high altitude
test.why: Mexico City's altitude of about 2,240 meters helped jumps and sprints.

test.q: Why did FINA ban full-body polyurethane suits from 2010?
choices: Critics said records measured suits, not swimmers
They were unsafe in cold water
test.why: Dozens of records fell in the suits, which critics called technological doping.

choices: IOC first tests athletes at the Games
test.why: Maris hit 61 in 1961, before testing in 1968, Johnson in 1988 and WADA in 1999.

test.q: Why do Cobb's hit totals differ between books?
choices: Researchers found a 1910 game counted twice, but MLB kept the old total
His records were erased for doping
test.why: Research gives 4,189; MLB's official record stays at 4,191.

test.q: What changed in baseball's records in May 2024?
choices: Maris was given the sole record
Negro Leagues statistics entered MLB's official records
test.why: After the 2020 recognition, MLB added the statistics in 2024, making Josh Gibson the career batting leader.

test.q: What do the Frick ruling, the javelin redesign and the 2010 swimsuit ban share?
choices: All were made by the IOC
Each shows an authority deciding which marks can be compared
test.why: In each case a governing body decided how records from different conditions would be counted.

write.prompt: Argue a position: Is a sports record a fact or an argument? Cite at least three dated events from this unit, such as the 1961 Frick ruling, the 1977 timing rule, the 1986 javelin redesign, the 2010 swimsuit ban or MLB's 2020 Negro Leagues decision, and explain what each shows.
tips: Name each document, body and year you cite, such as the IAAF rule of 1977 or the Sports Broadcasting Act of 1961.
Say who had the authority to decide, and what they decided.
Compare conditions before and after each change instead of judging the athletes.
Use unit terms such as ratify, specification, wind-aided and official record.
End with one sentence that answers the question directly.
